## **What is a lot number?**


A lot number is a unique identifier assigned to a group of products or materials manufactured or processed together under the same conditions.


Lot numbers allow businesses to track batches of products that are produced together. They ensure traceability: if a product is recalled, the rest of the items in that batch can easily be identified due to them sharing the same lot number.


Product recall is much more manageable with the use of lot numbers. These items can be quickly isolated and taken out of circulation or removed from the lineup without impacting other inventory.


Related, lot numbers enable better quality control. Businesses can track exactly which products have issues, are receiving customer complaints or generally aren’t selling well. This allows for fast action.


## **Lot number vs. serial number vs. SKU**


These identifiers can be easy to mix up, but we’re here to clarify.


### **Lot numbers**


As discussed, lot numbers are used to identify a batch of products manufactured under the same conditions.


**When to use lot numbers:**


- When recall, quality control and legal compliance are of utmost importance to the business.
- Lot numbers are commonly used in industries that distribute regulated products, perishables or other items that require quality control and tracking.
- **Examples:** pharmaceuticals, cosmetics and food.


### **Serial numbers**


A serial number is a unique identifier for individual products or units, and no two serial numbers are the same.


**When to use serial numbers:**


- When individual items need to be tracked.
- Serial numbers are often used for high-value items or for complex products such as services or warranty tracking.
- **Examples:** vehicles, electronics, appliances or machinery.


### **SKU (stock keeping unit)**


A[SKU](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/sku-numbers/) is a code used by retailers to identify specific products or variations of products for inventory purposes.


**When to use SKUs:**


- For internally categorizing inventory in order to track the quantity and location of units for sale.
- When products need to be differentiated by characteristics including size, color, model. Etc.
- **Examples:** any business that manages multiple versions of a product.


## **Lot number vs. serial number vs. SKU: comparison table**


When it comes to comparing lot number vs serial number, the key distinction is batch-level tracking versus unit-level tracking. While a lot number may cover thousands of shared items, a serial number belongs exclusively to one specific device or product.


When looking at SKU vs lot number, a SKU identifies a product or variant in a seller’s catalog, such as a blue medium t-shirt, while a lot number identifies a batch of that product. Multiple units can share a lot number or SKU, but each item has its own serial number.


Below, we’ve put together a quick comparison table highlighting key differences between lot numbers, serial numbers and SKUs.


**Lot number** **Serial number** **SKU**


**Identifies** A batch of items produced together One individual item A specific product type, model or variant


**Quantity** A batch of items per number One item per number Many items per number


**Purpose** Quality control, expiry management and recalls Warranty validation, theft tracking, repairs and authentication Inventory tracking, reordering and sales management


**Assigned by** Manufacturer Manufacturer Retailer or merchant


**Example** Food, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics Electronics, vehicles, medical devices, appliances, machinery Retail merchandise, ecommerce cataloging


## **Why are lot numbers important for businesses?**


There are a few reasons why lot numbers are important for businesses.


### **Traceability**


With lot numbers, lot number on products and lot number tracking, businesses can track and trace products from end to end, from the start of the supply chain to when the product is on the shelf. Businesses can use lots to track when products shipped, when they were manufactured, who received the products and more. Plus, it goes even further with lot number tracking to trace the producer of raw materials involved, date and location of production and more.


Traceability is extra important for businesses that must abide by legal mandates and compliance laws such as food and pharmaceuticals. If a recall is required, businesses can quickly take every product with that lot number on products off the shelf.


### **Compliance**


Lot numbers play a significant role in compliance. Regulatory requirements in the industries we mentioned above, for example–pharmaceuticals and food–are enforced by various regulatory bodies. That includes the FDA (Food and Drug Administration) and the EMA (European Medicines Agency).


These bodies mandate strict traceability, quality control, detailed records, supply chain accountability and more. Businesses have to provide this information and ensure it is up-to-date at all times in order to prevent recall disasters, for one thing. That’s why lot numbers are so important–they ensure traceability at all times.


### **Quality control**


Effective quality control can help prevent recalls. Lot numbers give businesses insight into the quality of batches. Ultimately, this helps them to identify consistency and quality issues. Many industries that are required to use lots carry out batch testing to ensure these products are up to standard before they are circulated.


Suppliers are also often part of quality control evaluations, which may reduce the likelihood of defects, contamination and other common issues that lead to recalls. Lot numbers help businesses isolate affected batches, ensuring that other inventory isn’t impacted or lost as a result. This also helps maintain customer trust and confidence. Businesses must ensure they document all quality control measures, with a lot information included.


## **Where and how to find a lot number**


Lot numbers can be found on the packaging of the products.They are stamped onto packaging on the factory line during sealing, so they look printed after the fact rather than part of the original label design.


When figuring out exactly where to find lot number on product packaging, your best bet is checking right next to the expiration date. Typically, lot numbers are prefixed with **LOT** , **Lot No** , **BATCH** or simply **L** or **B** , followed by a short string of numbers, letters or both.


Here’s how to find lot number on product packaging based on packaging type:


- **Bottles and jars (liquids, supplements, condiments):** base, back label, neck or cap
- **Boxes and cartons (medications, cereal, dry goods):** bottom flap, side panel or near the barcode
- **Flexible pouches and bags (frozen foods, pet foods, snacks):** back panel, sealed edge or near the expiration date
- **Cans (beverages, preserves):** bottom, lid or side seam
- **Blister packs (pills, lozenges):** foil edge around the pills
- **Tubes (cosmetics, toothpaste):** crimped or sealed end, back label or near the cap


## **How to create a lot number**


### **1. Choose a format for your lot number**


The format you use should contain meaningful information such as:


- **Batch number:** a unique number assigned to a batch of products
- **Date of production:** helps trace product manufacturing
- **Location code:** helps you identify where it came from
- **Product/category code:** to distinguish between different product lines
- **Supplier code:** especially useful if you have several different suppliers


Example lot number formats:


- Location-YYYYMMDD-Batch#
- Supplier-YYYYMMDD-Batch#
- Batch#-YYYYMMDD-Product


As you can likely tell in the above examples, the lot number doesn’t have to include all the information we’ve listed. As long as you have a system in place that works for you, any combination of information–or anything else you deem relevant–is fine to use.


### **2. Choose which information to include**


Your lot numbers are dependent on your unique business needs, as well as your industry. That’s why you may choose to use a combination of different elements, based on factors such as:


- **Expiration dates:** these are highly useful for food and pharmaceuticals, and may be legally required as well, depending on your jurisdiction.
- **Lot size:** this is the number of units that were produced or manufactured together. Use distinct batch numbers if the items were manufactured in distinct lots.
- **Supplier information:** this will allow you to easily identify the supplier from which the items originated.


### **3. Use a consistent format**


Now that you know what kind of information you should include, it’s time to decide on a consistent format. Establish a uniform process to generate lot numbers. Doing so will prevent confusion and duplication while ensuring your lots are organized. The formats could be styled as follows:


- **Data-based formats:** these numbers use dates as the main identifier
- **Sequential formats:** simple formats that don’t use a date
- **Combination formats:** a mix of several elements


### **4. Start automating your lot numbers**


You’ll save yourself a lot of time by using an[inventory management system](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/pos/retail/inventory-management-software/) that provides automatic tracking and built-in tools for generation of lot numbers. With this, you can guarantee that the numbers are unique–no duplication of data.


### **5. Ensure proper recordkeeping**


Earlier, we discussed how many industries are legally required to provide detailed records of lot number and batch information. Keep an organized record of relevant lot information, including date manufactured, materials used, location, etc. Automating these administrative processes lets you avoid issues that occur as a result of natural human errors.


### **6. Apply lot numbers to products**


Comply with regulatory requirements to properly label products with lots. These numbers should be clearly marked on each item. This process may be done through barcodes, printed labels, QR codes, or as part of the manufacturing process by the supplier. As always, keep digital records.


## **How to use lot numbers**


Lot numbers should be integrated into inventory management systems. Here’s how this is achieved:


- Use an inventory management system that enables you to generate, store and track lot numbers automatically. Each batch should be logged in the system with all relevant details.
- We also mentioned earlier that automating lot number generation can save you a lot of time, especially if you configure your inventory system to do this.
- With all lot numbers logged, the system should link back to all the data you need for traceability purposes.


When it comes to labeling, remember to:


- Use standardized labeling practices across facilities and suppliers. This ensures identification and traceability.
- Ensure several points of labeling. Include the lot number on the external packaging, on containers and in digital records throughout the supply chain.


### **Scenarios where lot numbers are crucial**


- **Product recalls:** Lot numbers minimize the impact on unaffected products because they allow for targeted recall.
- **Inventory audits:** Since lot numbers allow specific batches to be tracked throughout the supply chain–from production to warehousing to sales–stock counts can be easily verified.
- **Supply chain management:** Lot numbers allow product origins to be easily traced, improving supply chain visibility. Not only does this reduce risks, but it improves supplier accountability.


## **What are the benefits of lot tracking?**


We’ve touched on this throughout, but we really want to hammer home the benefits of lot tracking. Let’s go over them one more time.


### **Quality assurance**


Businesses can maintain product quality with lot tracking. This is because defects can be linked to specific batches, facilitating targeted recalls. Lot numbers minimize disruption and costs due to quality issues. That means only the affected products are removed from circulation. Not only that, but lot tracking can help businesses identify recurring issues. Ultimately, this results in better monitoring of production processes and the subsequent ability to make improvements.


### **Compliance**


Having a traceable history of each batch produced is key for adhering to industry regulations. Plus, detailed and accurate records streamline the process for regulatory audits, ensuring nothing is missed. As well, lot tracking minimizes the risks of fines and penalties associated with non-compliance because products meet the required standards.


### **Efficiency**


Lot tracking facilitates[first-in, first-out inventory management](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/what-is-fifo/) , ensuring that older products are used first. This is especially important for perishable products and pharmaceuticals. Additionally, production planning is streamlined. With insights into batch performance, businesses can make revenue-boosting decisions and allocate resources more accurately. Inventory management as a whole is streamlined because lot tracking enables efficient and accurate stock counts.

### **Product recalls**


Product recalls can happen to any retailer. That’s why it’s crucial to stay prepared with product lot tracking. When there’s a manufacturing defect, product lot tracking allows retailers to provide thorough tracking and handle large-scale recalls efficiently.


## **How can I check the expiration date of lot numbers?**


It’s important to check the expiration date of the lot number on products to maintain oversight and improve visibility across your inventory. This helps ensure you’re always selling the best product possible.


- **Print the expiry date:** If you know the year, month and location of the product, you can create labels that include this information along with the lot number on products, then attach them to each item.
- **Use a barcode scanner:** You can also use a[barcode scanner](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/pos/retail/scanner/) that includes lot number tracking directly within the code to quickly access expiration details.
- **Leverage software:** Use the data in your system for lot number tracking to monitor product information and expiration dates automatically.

Lot numbers are an important part of inventory management for many businesses. They help keep you compliant, increase efficiency, improve quality assurance and more.

## **FAQ**


### **What can a lot number tell you?**


A lot number is a unique code that identifies a batch of products made under the same conditions. It tells you key details like when and where the items were produced, which materials were used and their expiration dates. In other words, what a lot means on products is the group or batch they belong to, helping businesses track quality, manage recalls and maintain compliance across the supply chain.


### **How is a lot number different from a serial number?**


A lot number is an identifier that groups products manufactured together, known as a batch, whereas a serial number is unique to each individual item, enabling specific units to be tracked.


### **Where should I place the lot number on my products?**


A lot number should be placed in highly visible areas on product packaging, labels or containers. As well, place them on both external and internal packaging.


### **How does lot tracking improve inventory management?**


Lot tracking improves inventory management through ease of traceability, which reduces waste and enables targeted recalls. It also improves quality assurance, ensures regulatory compliance, and reduces waste.
